title: Adaptive kernel selection: INT8 vs FP8 case notes
summary: Exploratory notes and microbenchmark results for an adaptive kernel-selection strategy that chooses per-layer execution kernels at runtime across INT8 (GPTQ), AWQ variants, and FP8 to balance latency, memory, and quality for encoder-decoder workloads.
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures an experimental sweep and early prototype for runtime-adaptive kernel selection. Motivation: we see layer-to-layer variability in numeric sensitivity and kernel throughput; a one-size-fits-all kernel (e.g. tiled-int8) leaves tail-latency on the table and sometimes causes avoidable quality regressions. The idea: choose kernel per-layer (or layer-group) at model load time and allow fast fallback at inference time if capacity/latency SLOs require it.

Scope and constraints:
- Models: internal T5-style encoder-decoder family (11B and 3B variants used for these tests). Not decoder-only (we expect encoder layers to behave differently).
- Quantization formats: GPTQ-int8, AWQ-int4->int8 runpaths (AWQ-enabled kernels), and FP8 (recent fp8-backed kernels).
- Kernels profiled: tiled-int8-v1, tiled-int8-v2 (cache-friendly), awq-fused-matmul, fp8-fused-attn, fused-attn-opt-v1 (float fallback), matmul-simd-vec, and small-batch-vec-optimized.
- Hardware: A100-80GB and a mixed pool with H100 dev nodes (results below split by device).
- Workload: interactive generation (seq_out up to 512 tokens), batch sizes tested: 1, 2, 4. Arrival process: Poisson client sim with average QPS that stresses p99.
- Measurement tools: nvprof/nsys sampling for kernel times, our request-replay harness (client-sim v2), and token-level accounting from console traces.

Methodology:
1) Microbench each kernel on representative layer shapes (embed, feedforward large dim, attention key/value dims) and record median and 95/99 kernel execution times for a single forward pass (no KV cache).
2) Run end-to-end inference for a small set of prompt templates (code, instruction, summarization) to capture quality differences (log-perplexity/human-eval proxies). For speed we use perplexity and a small reference prompt-set for EM/ROUGE where applicable.
3) Evaluate adaptive policy: per-layer throughput model (t/ms), numeric-sensitivity estimate (from post-quantization calibration PASSED fraction), and memory footprint delta. Policy chooses kernel that minimizes latency subject to quality delta < threshold.

Representative microbench results (A100, 512-token forward, median of 50 runs):
- tiled-int8-v1: median 4.6 ms / layer; p99 8.2 ms; mem 1.1 GB; quality delta (vs fp32): +0.8 perplexity
- tiled-int8-v2: median 4.1 ms / layer; p99 6.9 ms; mem 1.05 GB; quality delta: +0.9
- awq-fused-matmul: median 3.8 ms / layer; p99 7.6 ms; mem 0.95 GB; quality delta: +1.4 (some attention heads affected)
- fp8-fused-attn: median 5.2 ms / layer; p99 9.5 ms; mem 1.3 GB; quality delta: +0.3
- fused-attn-opt-v1 (float): median 7.5 ms / layer; p99 12.1 ms; mem 2.0 GB; quality delta: 0.0
- small-batch-vec-optimized: median 6.0 ms / layer (batch=1); improves to 3.2 ms at batch=4

Interpretation of microbench:
- AWQ kernels are fastest on compute-heavy feedforward matmuls but have higher per-layer quality delta on certain attention weight distributions (sparse-simulated heads).
- FP8 kernels are slightly slower than the fastest INT8 kernels but offer markedly better quality stability; memory usage is higher but still cheaper than full fp32.
- p99 behavior diverges from median in kernels with vector-lane code-path variance; tiled-int8-v2 reduced jitter significantly versus v1.

End-to-end traces (T5-11B, A100, batch=1, generation length 512; numbers are median across prompt templates):
- Baseline (single kernel tiled-int8-v2 everywhere): median latency 420 ms; p99 820 ms; tokens/sec 190; perplexity delta vs fp32: +1.0
- FP8 everywhere: median latency 520 ms; p99 980 ms; tokens/sec 155; perplexity delta: +0.2
- Adaptive policy (per-layer policy, threshold perplexity +0.5): median 380 ms; p99 670 ms; tokens/sec 210; perplexity delta: +0.45
- Conservative adaptive (threshold +0.2): median 430 ms; p99 730 ms; tokens/sec 185; perplexity delta: +0.18

Key observations from end-to-end runs:
- Adaptive routing beats single-kernel baselines on both median latency and tokens/sec while keeping quality within configured thresholds.
- The p99 gains are larger than median gains; adaptive policy avoided pathological slow kernels on a subset of layers (particularly some attention blocks) under the live scheduler.
- FP8 everywhere gives best-quality fidelity but the latency and memory cost is non-trivial; FP8 is a good conservative option for customers with tight quality constraints.

Edge cases and failure modes:
- Model variants with attention head permutations (we have ~3 checkpoints) show inconsistent AWQ sensitivity: some checkpoints suffer >2.5 perplexity delta with AWQ. Need per-checkpoint sensitivity profiling.
- Cold start: kernel selection policy adds ~20-40ms to first request as we probe microbench for layer shapes. We can amortize by doing sampling during model load or using stored profiles in the catalog.
- Mixed-quant caches: KV cache encoded under different numeric formats requires conversion and adds ~1.8–3.5ms when crossing formats mid-inference. Adaptive policy must prefer consistent numeric format on hot-path unless benefit is high.

Prototype implementation notes:
- Policy inputs: layer_shape (d_model, d_ff, heads), static quant-sensitivity metric (derived from calibration set), runtime throughput counters, device type.
- Runtime is a small router that picks kernel id from an in-memory table (fast path: one array lookup per layer). Fallbacks are implemented via a fast jump-table; switching cost measured ~0.6ms on A100.
- Profiling bootstrap: run a per-node microbench at model load over canonical layer shapes; store profiles in node-local cache keyed by (device, kernel, layer-shape-hash).

Commands / harness snippets used (copyable):
- client-sim harness: ./client_sim --model t5-11b --prompt-set prompts/quality-100.txt --max-tokens 512 --arrival poisson --qps 12 --batch-sizes 1,2,4 --policy adaptive-profiled
- microbench script: python microbench.py --kernel tiled-int8-v2 --shape 4096:16384:32 --device a100 --iters 200
- collect traces: nsys profile --output nsight-adapt-jan --sample cpu --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi -- ./serving-node --run-bench 

Representative raw_results (trimmed):
- t5-11b A100 baseline tiled-int8-v2: median_end2end 420ms; p99 820ms; tokens_sec 190; perplex_delta +1.0
- t5-11b A100 adaptive: median_end2end 380ms; p99 670ms; tokens_sec 210; perplex_delta +0.45
- t5-3b mixed node fp8: median 210ms; p99 340ms; tokens_sec 285; perplex_delta +0.25

Conclusions so far:
- Adaptive per-layer kernel selection is promising: it reduces median latency and p99 for interactive generation while allowing controllable quality budgets.
- AWQ-based kernels are attractive for throughput, but we must be conservative on attention-sensitive checkpoints. Per-checkpoint sensitivity profiling is required before enabling AWQ in production for a customer.
- FP8 gives low quality regret but higher latency and memory; it should be offered as a safe default for enterprise/private customers who opt-in for quality protection.
- Caching of node profiles and doing warm microbench at model load removes most cold-start overhead.

Next steps (short term):
- Expand microbench grid to cover more layer shapes (esp. non-uniform attention heads) and H100 variants. (Action: Diego, 1 week)
- Add per-checkpoint sensitivity run to onboarding pipeline and store sensitivity flags in model catalog. (Action: Aisha, 2 weeks)
- Integrate KV-format compatibility check in adaptive policy. If switching format mid-request, require net latency benefit > X ms (TBD). (Action: Marcus)
- Run 72-hour soak with client-sim at QPS=peak to validate scheduler stability and fallback correctness. (Action: SRE)

Unresolved questions / open design choices:
- Threshold selection for acceptable quality delta: how to translate perplexity deltas into customer-facing SLOs? Need product input (product-hosted-api).
- How to safely allow AWQ on multi-tenant Dedicated deployments where model checkpoints vary? Could gate AWQ behind reserved-capacity feature flags.
- How to present mixed-format KV-cache transitions in observability dashboard (show estimated conversion cost).

Appendix: quick primer on numeric sensitivity metric used in this sweep:
- For each layer we run a small calibration pass with n=64 calibration sequences; compute distribution of per-token logit differences between fp32 and quantized kernels; derive the fraction of tokens with abs(delta_logits) > threshold (0.02). We call the complement the PASSED fraction. Layers with PASSED < 0.92 flagged as "sensitive".

Notes to self / TODO in this doc:
- Add H100 microbench numbers (haven't finished trace parsing).
- Push prototype router as a feature branch and add unit tests for format-switch fallback.
- Schedule a short whiteboard with product for policy threshold mapping.

raw_results: A100 microbench summary (median of 50 runs): tiled-int8-v2 4.1ms median, p99 6.9ms; awq-fused 3.8ms median, p99 7.6ms; fp8-fused 5.2ms median p99 9.5ms. E2E T5-11B batch1 baseline tiled-int8-v2 median 420ms p99 820ms; adaptive median 380ms p99 670ms; fp8 median 520ms p99 980ms.
conclusions: Adaptive kernel selection reduces latency and p99 with controllable quality tradeoffs. AWQ needs per-checkpoint gating. FP8 is the conservative, higher-quality option. Profiles should be cached at model-load to avoid cold-starts.
